title: Event Delegation
subtopics: Delegation for tables, lists, and menus
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of event delegation in a jQuery application.
Apply delegating events to a parent in a small example and describe its expected result.
Verify the delegated selector parameter with an explicit test or browser observation.
status_note: Draft generated from the attached syllabus and official references; requires lesson-by-lesson technical review, local execution, accessibility checks, and editorial approval.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will work through event delegation with a focused jQuery example. The subtopics below preserve the supplied curriculum coverage and connect the API idea to a small browser interface.
content.why_it_matters: This topic is useful because it turns delegating events to a parent into a repeatable implementation choice. Use .on() for current event handling. Delegation allows a stable parent to handle events from future matching descendants, while event namespaces help cleanup.

task_acceptance_criteria: The implementation demonstrates event delegation using a current, documented approach.
The learner records the expected and actual behavior and checks at least one edge case.
The example preserves semantic HTML and does not render untrusted data as HTML.
The test setup and any runtime limitation are documented honestly.
hints: First identify which DOM nodes and runtime state are involved in event delegation.
Make one small change, inspect the resulting element or request, and compare it with the expected result.
If the result differs, check the selector, script order, browser console, event target, and relevant API documentation before adding more code.
content.expected_output: The stable list container handles clicks from current and future .task-remove descendants.
common_mistakes: Assuming a selector matched an element without checking the collection length.
Confusing jQuery collections with native DOM elements or live properties with markup attributes.
Using .html() with untrusted data or assuming client-side validation enforces server rules.
Treating a demo snippet as production-ready without testing failure and accessibility states.
